Action Plan:
1) Proceed with treatment for a likely eczema flare: initiate a stronger topical corticosteroid regimen and provide emollients to moisturize the skin; advise use in the bath/shower for the next 7–10 days and reassess response.
2) Address itching with an oral antihistamine: prescribe fexofenadine today (dose/route/frequency not documented); discuss over-the-counter options (loratadine or promethazine–Piriton) if needed.
3) Advise patient to keep a daily diary of symptoms and potential triggers (e.g., new skincare/shower products, soaps, detergents) to identify contributing factors.
4) Schedule follow-up in 7–10 days to evaluate response; return sooner if symptoms worsen or signs of infection develop.
5) Discuss possible differential diagnoses (allergic contact dermatitis, irritant dermatitis) and the role of triggers; plan to revisit diagnosis if there is poor response to therapy.
6) Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Note: A COVID-19 vaccine suitability assessment was not required in this visit.

- Onset/duration/progression: onset about 3–4 days ago (transcript notes 4 days ago); symptoms persistent and worsening, severe itch affecting sleep and concentration.
- Past medical history: history of eczema; past asthma (not currently treated).
- Medications: none currently; previously used an OTC steroid cream with no lasting benefit; no regular medications.
- Allergies: none.
- Social history: lives with flatmates; works as project manager at a pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; occasional alcohol use.
- Additional history: no fever, cough, or respiratory symptoms; no genital/ocular involvement reported; no urinary or systemic symptoms; no facial involvement; no bleeding or purulent discharge from skin.

Objective:

- No explicit exam findings beyond patient description and clinician remarks on skin type and distribution.

Assessment & Plan:
1) Issue: Acute eczema flare (atopic dermatitis) with multifocal pruritus and dry, cracked skin.
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis flare.
   - Consistent differential diagnoses (from DDx, aligned with transcript): Allergic contact dermatitis (Medium); Irritant contact dermatitis (Medium). Mycosis fungoides considered low likelihood; other systemic pruritus causes less likely given presentation.
   - Investigations planned: None at this time; monitor response to therapy. (No labs/imaging indicated by transcript.)
   - Treatment planned:
     - Stronger topical corticosteroid for flare management.
     - Emollients for daily skin moisturization (including use in bath/shower routine).
     - Antihistamine therapy for itch (fexofenadine prescribed today; discuss OTC options if needed; prior antihistamines attempted with limited effect).
     - Skin-care diary to identify potential triggers (new soaps, shower products, detergents, fabrics, etc.).
     - Follow-up in 7–10 days to assess response; escalate or adjust therapy if no improvement.
   - Referrals: None indicated at this time.

2) Issue: Trigger assessment and differential considerations (possible allergic or irritant dermatitis).
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Differential includes allergic contact dermatitis and irritant contact dermatitis (based on ddx, consistent with transcript).
   - Differential diagnoses (from DDx where consistent): Allergic contact dermatitis (Medium); Irritant contact dermatitis (Medium).
   - Investigations planned: Consider trigger diary; no patch testing or labs specified unless symptoms persist or worsen.
   - Treatment planned: Continue eczema-directed therapy; continue to monitor for triggers; consider adjusting products if diary identifies a likely contact irritant/allergen.
   - Referrals: None.

- Transcript-DDx conflicts: None identified; plan aligns with the DDx by prioritizing eczema flare and including plausible alternative dermatitis etiologies as differentials.
